newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia Grains-El Nino uncertainty dogs wheat.
newsitem.headline: Australia Grains-El Nino uncertainty dogs wheat.

text.p: Added uncertainty is emerging over how much wheat Australia will produce in 1997/98 due to the El Nino weather pattern, which forecasters said promises to inflict drought on some growing regions.

For now, the Australian Wheat Board (AWB) said it is sticking with an estimate of around 18 million tonnes, although the Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics (ABARE) has reiterated its forecast of only 16.3 million tonnes, based on the effects of El Nino.

Weather experts meeting in Melbourne have left little doubt a major El Nino event is forming in the tropical Pacific Ocean. The phenomenom has the potential to overshadow the previous El Nino of the the 1990s and could reach proportions of the 1982/83 one, which caused widespread drought in Australia.
However, the forecasts did little to rattle local futures trading last week at the Sydney Futures Exchange.
Wheat futures saw no significant movement, with prices unchanged or firmer by between A$2 and A$4 a tonne, depending on locaion, the AWB noted.
Central and southeastern New South Wales saw good rains over the previous weekend, easing concerns of drought in the region.

"The market however, is still focussed on the dry conditions of the Victorian and South Australian Mallee and Central Eyre Peninsula and some of these areas may turn to barley, although their planting window extends to the end of July, " the AWB said in its latest weekly grains report.
Old crop prices were underpinned by the tender results providing a price ceiling fro the trade around the low A$180 a tonne, deliverd to Port Kembla and Geelong, it said.

June rainfall across much of southern Australia was significantly below average, consistent with the near-extreme low value of the southern oscillation index (SOI) and other strong El Nino characteristics, Australia's Bureau of Meteorology has warned.

Expectations the El Nino effect will persist for the rest of 1997 means there is a strong chance of significantly drier-than-normal conditions will prevail in comining months across much of eastern Australia.

"In terms of the warming of the water and the southern oscillation index, it is on a par with the 1982/83 pattern," Tom Spence, head of the climate observing system for the World Meteorological Organisation said.
The southern oscillation index is a measure of the difference in air pressure between Tahiti and Darwin, Australia. A low index means drought.
